issue.issue_text: Whether the Revenue Officer had jurisdiction to entertain the dispute between the parties.

facts: A dispute arose between the appellants and the respondent, which was brought before a Revenue Officer.
The respondent contended that the Revenue Officer did not have the jurisdiction to entertain this dispute.
law: The court examined the Act that applied to the dispute.
The court also considered the relevant provisions regarding procedure and penalties contained in the 1948 Act.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the applicable Act, when read together with the procedural provisions of the 1948 Act, did in fact grant jurisdiction to the Revenue Officer to hear the dispute between the parties.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the respondent's contention that the Revenue Officer lacked jurisdiction. It held that the relevant statutes conferred authority on the Revenue Officer to entertain the dispute. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal and restored the original orders passed by the Revenue Officer.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him, as required by Article 311(2) of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant, a government servant, was subjected to a disciplinary inquiry on several charges.
At the start of the inquiry, he was asked to show cause why he should not be dismissed, removed, reduced, or subjected to other disciplinary action if the charges were proven.
The inquiring officer (Shri J. B. Tandon) found the appellant guilty and suggested the punishment of dismissal.
The competent authority (the Deputy Commissioner) accepted the report and confirmed the decision to dismiss the appellant.
The appellant was then dismissed without being given a further opportunity to make a representation against the specific punishment of dismissal after the finding of guilt was confirmed.
law: The Supreme Court interpreted the phrase 'reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken' in Article 311(2) of the Constitution to involve a two-stage process.
Stage 1: An opportunity must be given to the government servant to defend themselves against the charges during the inquiry. This is the stage to prove their innocence.

Stage 2: If the inquiry results in a finding of guilt and the competent authority proposes a specific punishment (like dismissal), a second and separate opportunity must be given to the servant to show cause against that particular punishment.
The Court held that merely informing the servant at the beginning of the inquiry that dismissal is a possible outcome is not sufficient to satisfy the requirements of the second stage.
application: The Court applied its two-stage interpretation to the appellant's case.
It found that while the appellant had an opportunity during the inquiry (Stage 1), he was denied the crucial second opportunity.
The 'action proposed' (dismissal) was only formally decided upon when the Deputy Commissioner accepted the inquiry report and confirmed the punishment.
The Court determined that it was at this point that the appellant was constitutionally entitled to be notified of the proposed penalty and be given a chance to argue against it.
Since this second opportunity was not provided, the procedure followed was deficient.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was not given the reasonable opportunity required by Article 311(2) because he was denied the second-stage opportunity to show cause against the specific punishment of dismissal after the competent authority had made its finding of guilt. Therefore, the constitutional protection was not fully afforded, the dismissal was invalid, and the Court accepted the appeal.

appellant_arguments: The Revenue Officer did not have jurisdiction to entertain the dispute.
respondent_arguments: The relevant Act, read together with the provisions of the 1948 Act, gave the Revenue Officer jurisdiction to entertain the dispute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him, as required by Article 311(2) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The opportunity to show cause should be given after the inquiry officer's findings have been considered and the punishment has been decided upon.
There should be two distinct inquiries: the first to establish guilt, and the second to determine the appropriate punishment, with a reasonable opportunity to show cause at each stage.
The appellant was not provided with a copy of the inquiry officer's report.
respondent_arguments: A single inquiry was sufficient because the appellant was aware from the beginning that dismissal was a possible outcome, and therefore he was showing cause against the proposed action throughout the inquiry.

cases.principle: No 'action is proposed' within the meaning of the statute until a definite conclusion has been come to on the charges, and the actual punishment to follow is provisionally determined on. The civil servant must be told of the charges against him and the proposed punishment, so he can show cause against that particular punishment.

The words 'against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him' require a definite proposal by an authority to dismiss or reduce in rank a civil servant. The civil servant must be told of this proposal and the grounds for it, and be given a reasonable opportunity to present his case against the proposed action.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: No action is considered 'proposed' under Article 311(2) of the Constitution until a definite conclusion has been reached on the charges against a civil servant, and the specific punishment to follow has been provisionally determined. The civil servant must then be given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against that specific, provisionally determined punishment.
obiter: Varadachariar, J., in his dissenting judgment took much the same view on this point as did the High Court.

If any question arises whether it is reasonably practicable to give to any person an opportunity of showing cause under clause (2), the decision thereon of the authority empowered to dismiss or remove such person or to reduce him in rank, as the case may be shall be final.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the 'reasonable opportunity of showing cause' required by Article 311(2) of the Constitution is not a single event but a two-stage process. It is not sufficient that an employee is aware from the start of an inquiry that dismissal is a possible outcome. After the inquiry into the charges is complete and the authority has provisionally decided upon the employee's guilt and the specific punishment to be imposed, the employee must be given a second, distinct opportunity to show cause against that proposed punishment. This second opportunity is only reasonable if the employee is supplied with a copy of the inquiry officer's findings and the grounds for the proposed action.
legal_tests_applied: The 'reasonable opportunity' test under Article 311(2) requires a two-stage process: first, an inquiry into the charges where the employee can defend against the allegations of misconduct, and second, a subsequent opportunity to show cause against the specific punishment proposed after a finding of guilt.

For the second stage opportunity to be reasonable, the employee must be informed of the proposed action, the grounds for it, and the results of the initial inquiry, including the findings of the enquiring officer, so they can make an informed representation against the proposed penalty.

policy_considerations: In order for the opportunity to show cause to be a reasonable one, it is necessary that the government servant has the opportunity to argue that they are not guilty of any misconduct that would merit punishment. This requires that the servant be informed of the charges and the evidence against them, as 'it is only then that he will be able to put forward his defence'.

A reasonable opportunity must allow the government servant to show that the evidence against them 'is not worthy of credence or consideration,' which necessitates being informed of the findings of the inquiry upon which the proposed punishment is based.
